finding.claim: reset_password_loose compares the stored reset token to the supplied token with loose `==`. PHP type juggling can make unequal tokens compare equal, so an attacker can reset another user's password without the real token. Examples: both strings are numeric-looking, such as a stored token like "0e12345" and a supplied "0e999", which both evaluate as 0 in scientific notation; or, on PHP < 8, a non-numeric stored string against integer 0 supplied via JSON or a typed parameter.
finding.source: Unauthenticated caller-supplied $email (victim's address) and $token (and $new, the new password).
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw = ... WHERE email = ... at reset.php:5-6, an account takeover through password overwrite.

trace.note: Fetches the stored token for the attacker-chosen email.
`$row['token'] == $token` uses loose comparison, so "0e.." strings and, on PHP < 8, int 0 match.
The victim's password hash is overwritten with the attacker's chosen password.

finding.guards_checked: No type cast on $token, no strict `===` or hash_equals, and no expiry or rate limiting in this function. Queries are built with $db->quote(), so there is no SQL injection. The sibling reset_password() at line 14 uses hash_equals with a (string) cast, which confirms the loose version is the flawed variant. I could not see a caller, since only this file exists, so whether the loose function is actually reachable is unconfirmed. Exploitability depends on token format (a stored token matching ^0e\d+$ is probabilistic, about 1 in 10^2-3 for random hex tokens) or on PHP version.

verdict.guard_found: none (no cast, strict compare, hash_equals, expiry or rate limit in reset_password_loose; SQL is quoted, so no injection)
verdict.reason: reset.php:4 compares `$row['token'] == $token` loosely and lines 5-6 then overwrite the password for the attacker-chosen email with no other guard, so a stored token matching ^0e\d+$ (or int 0 on PHP < 8) is bypassable. Exploitability is probabilistic and depends on token format and PHP version, and no caller exists in this directory, so reachability is unconfirmed.

finding.claim: Both reset functions never expire or invalidate the reset token. There is no expiry timestamp check and no DELETE of the resets row after a successful reset, so a leaked or old token stays valid and can be reused to reset the password again, repeatedly. There is also no attempt limiting, so tokens can be brute-forced online.
finding.source: Anyone holding an old, leaked or guessed token, or able to guess tokens by repeated calls with a victim's $email.
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw ... at reset.php:15-16 (and 5-6).

trace.note: SELECT token only, with no created_at or expiry column consulted.
The comparison succeeds on any matching token regardless of age or prior use.
The password is updated, and no statement removes the token afterward.

finding.guards_checked: hash_equals provides constant-time comparison but no expiry, single-use or throttling. No other files exist to show these controls enforced elsewhere (for example by the caller), so this is a plausible design flaw rather than a confirmed one.

verdict.guard_found: hash_equals constant-time comparison (reset.php:14) only; no expiry, single-use deletion, or attempt throttling in this file; no other files exist.
verdict.reason: reset.php:13-16 selects only the token and, after a hash_equals match, updates the password with no expiry check or DELETE of the resets row, so the token is reusable indefinitely; the file does not show callers, so the throttling and brute-force part cannot be checked, but the non-expiry and non-invalidation parts are accurate.
